findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new getClient code calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time error (and a runtime ReferenceError if it were to build), so the Salesforce calendar service is broken by this PR.

findings.title: Sync endpoint response is returned as a raw fetch Response without checking status or parsing the body
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT and returns the raw `Response` object. It never checks `response.ok` and never calls `response.json()`. Callers then break: for example `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;` — a fetch Response has no `.data`, so this throws TypeError whenever sync mode is on. Similarly office365video/webex call `handleErrorsJson(response)` and others call `await resp.json()`, which would consume the body of an un-checked response. Token refresh silently fails for every integration when the feature is enabled.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema corrupts stored credentials: computed keys don't do what's intended, unknown fields are stripped, and a fake refresh_token is injected
findings.body: In zod, computed keys in an object literal like `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` do not create a catch-all rule for 'any property that is a number'; they just produce a literal (garbage) key. So in sync mode the schema effectively becomes `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), ... })`, which (a) strips every other field from the parsed result by default — so `refreshTokenResponse.data` returned to callers contains only `access_token`, dropping `expiry_date`/`expires_in`/scope that callers then persist (e.g. Google stores the result via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, wiping the real refresh token and expiry from the credential), and (b) line 26 then writes the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token when none is present, permanently corrupting the stored credential so subsequent real refreshes fail with invalid_grant.

findings.title: Passes credentialId instead of the Cal.com userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential's database id as the third argument, but that parameter is `userId` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. The parent platform will receive a credential id instead of a user id and will either 404 or refresh tokens for the wrong user. Every other integration passes `credential.userId`; this one should capture `credential.userId` in biginAuth and pass that.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality
findings.body: The header value is compared to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==`. This is a timing-safe-comparison candidate: use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) for a shared secret guarding credential writes. Additionally the secret check does not guard against both values being empty strings in a misconfigured deployment (empty header === empty env passes), and there is no method restriction or rate limiting on an endpoint that writes OAuth credentials.

findings.title: Zod parse and decrypt errors bubble up as unhandled 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`, `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw on invalid input (malformed body, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext). Since the handler has no try/catch, callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400; a misconfigured sender has no way to distinguish bad payload from server failure, and the webhook sender will likely retry forever.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create race allows duplicate credentials for the same user/app
findings.body: The endpoint does `findFirst` and then `create` without a transaction or unique constraint on (userId, appId). Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app both miss the findFirst and both create, leaving two credentials where downstream code uses `findFirst` and silently picks one. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` on a unique compound key (add one if missing) or wrap in a transaction with serializable isolation.

findings.title: isExpired compares expiry_date against +new Date() (milliseconds) but other services use seconds — unchanged inconsistency now matters more
findings.body: `isExpired = (expiryDate) => expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())` is correct here because expiry_date is stored in ms in this file, but office365calendar's own service stores `expires_in` in seconds and compares against seconds. With credentials now being pushed in from an external platform via the webhook, the expiry semantics (seconds vs ms) of the synced keys are undocumented and differ per integration, so externally-synced credentials will be treated as expired (or never expiring) depending on the app. The sync contract in the PR description only says 'access token and expiry date' without specifying units.
